newsitem.title: USA: Two U.S. Democratic senators fault Mexico on drugs.
newsitem.headline: Two U.S. Democratic senators fault Mexico on drugs.

text.p: Two Democratic senators on Tuesday urged President Bill Clinton not to certify Mexico as an ally in fighting drugs, saying it had not fully cooperated with Washington in stopping drug trafficking.

Senators Dianne Feinstein of California and Robert Torricelli of New Jersey -- Democratic Party allies of Clinton from states with significant Hispanic populations -- urged him to reassess the longstanding U.S. approval of Mexico's anti-drug efforts.
Clinton must announce by Saturday whether to certify Mexico and 31 other countries as U.S. allies in the fight against drugs.

Countries which do not pass the test and are "decertified" face U.S. economic sanctions. A third option would be a "vital national interests" certification, a waiver reserved for governments that fail to meet the standards but are deemed too important to hit with sanctions.
"I believe the evidence is overwhelming and can lead to no decision other than the decertification of Mexico," Feinstein said in a letter to Clinton.
"It would send a strong signal to Mexico and the world that the United States will not tolerate lack of cooperation in the fight against narcotics, even from close friends and allies."

Torricelli said in a letter to Clinton: "While I understand the sensitivity of the issue demands that this country proceed delicately, I would ask that you consider sending a tough message to the Mexican government and drug traffickers."
Washington was surprised last week when Mexico dismissed its top anti-narcotics official, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez, charging that he had ties to a drug kingpin.
